Vary the cache key by the response's Vary header and VaryByQueryKeys ## Description Stacked on #70891. Internal only. Other policies keep `DefaultOutputCacheEntryStrategy` and locking. Issues.Title: Output Caching: internal policy with Response Caching semantics
Issues.Body:
Part of #62728. Depends on dotnet/aspnetcore#70885.

An internal `ResponseCachingPolicy` for Output Caching, applying the HTTP caching semantics of Response Caching. The rules are ported one by one from `ResponseCachingPolicyProvider`:

- request: only `GET`/`HEAD` without `Authorization`; `no-cache` and `Pragma: no-cache` skip the lookup; `no-store` skips storage; `min-fresh`, `max-age`, `max-stale` decide freshness
- response: only `200` responses marked `public`, without `no-store`, `no-cache`, `private`, `Set-Cookie` or `Vary: *`; lifetime from `s-maxage`, `max-age`, `Expires`, otherwise 10s

For example, an endpoint setting `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3`:

| Request | Response Caching | Output Caching default policy |
|---|---|---|
| `Cache-Control: no-cache` | endpoint runs | served from cache |
| 4s later | endpoint runs | served from cache (60s default) |

Response Caching's test suite is ported to a new `Microsoft.AspNetCore.NewResponseCaching.Tests` project, running against Output Caching with this policy. Tests depending on `Vary` and `VaryByQueryKeys` stay skipped until the next issue.

Issues.Title: Output Caching: internal preparation for a Response Caching compatible policy
Issues.Body:
Part of #62728.

Internal changes in `OutputCacheMiddleware` needed by a policy applying Response Caching semantics. No public API, no behavior change for existing policies.

**1. Policies can mark a cached entry as stale**

`IsCacheEntryFresh` is set after the `ServeFromCacheAsync` policies run, so it overwrites their decision (e.g. a request sending `Cache-Control: max-age=0` is still served from cache):

```csharp
foreach (var policy in policies)
{
    await policy.ServeFromCacheAsync(context, ...);
}

context.IsCacheEntryFresh = true; // set before the loop instead
```

**2. Policies can set the expiration from the response**

The entry lifetime is fixed when the response headers are finalized (first body write), before `ServeResponseAsync` policies can read e.g. `Cache-Control: max-age=3` from the produced response. It should be recomputed from `ResponseExpirationTimeSpan` right before the entry is stored.

**3. Entry storage seam**

An internal `IOutputCacheEntryStrategy` wrapping the two store calls of the middleware (lookup and store). `DefaultOutputCacheEntryStrategy` is today's code, moved as is. This allows a different storage layout for the Response Caching policy (needed for `Vary`) without changing the middleware flow.

Issues.Body:
### Agent assessment Self-reported assessment, not an independent review. Assessed revision: `bab44ad12fec6b3853a396a197e32488ecf31451` | Dimension | Assessment | Rationale | |---|---|---| | Change confidence | 8.5/10 | ↑ Regression fixtures reproduce the review findings at the previous revision and pass against the updated source and generated workflow.
↑ Hosted fixtures exercised publication, a rename anchor, and moved-head rejection.
↑ A 43-file Components replay read scoped guidance and published an advisory review.
↓ Hosted .NET builds and publication at the inline ceiling were not exercised. | # Run /review from the frozen pull request checkout - [ ] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md). - [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable. - [ ] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable. - [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue. Run advisory reviews against a frozen pull request checkout. ## Description Use the native repository checkout and `code-review` skill with the frozen head, base tip, and merge base. Read existing feedback using GitHub's read-only `pull_requests` and `repos` toolsets. Findings without a reliable anchor go in the review summary; findings beyond 20 eligible inline comments go there as well, without trimming the structured result. The agent can use the shell inside the workflow sandbox after Git checkout credentials have been cleaned. Reviews still publish only through native safe outputs, behind the checkout pin check, both live-head checks, commit-specific attribution, the discarded-item filter, and threat detection. Transcript verification rejects publication calls from nested agents, and preflight filters discarded summary findings even when inline findings survive. Set `footer: false` because the default footer adds a workflow run link and model attribution to published output. ## Validation - `gh aw compile pull-request-review --approve` — passed. The baseline compile without `--approve` also passed, so there was no approval diagnostic. The SDK setup action was removed; the GitHub token references already existed. - `node --test .github\workflows\tests\pull-request-review-*.test.mjs` — passed against the workflow source and generated lock (25 transcript cases and 197 publication cases). - Hosted fixtures confirmed a body-only `COMMENT`, a mixed review anchored to an added line in a renamed file, and rejection before inference or publication when the PR moved after freezing. A staged run reached the end of paginated feedback, distinguished main and nested tool events, and skipped already-reported findings. - A 43-file Components replay read path-scoped guidance and published one advisory review with three inline comments. Detection passed. - Retains the existing ceilings of 150 reviewer credits and 200 detection credits. Real PRs using subagents may cost more than small fixtures; an older multi-agent workflow averaged 212.7 credits per review and is not directly comparable. Issue: N/A (workflow update).

## Summary

`WebViewManager.StaticWebAssetsLoader.ResolveRelativeToAssembly()` accesses `Assembly.Location`, which triggers `IL3000` trimming/single-file warnings in single-file deployments—most notably when publishing Blazor Hybrid apps with Native AOT (`PublishAot=true`).

We explored several fixes in #70875 (split out from the Native AOT WebView prototype in #70863) and closed that PR without choosing a single approach so we can align on the right trade-offs first.

## Motivation and goals

The [`WebViewManager` constructor](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/5d963d3a8e6dea79d039ec11f50ecef55df1f0ae/src/Components/WebView/WebView/src/WebViewManager.cs#L46-L53) unconditionally calls `StaticWebAssetsLoader.UseStaticWebAssets(fileProvider)`, which resolves `<assembly>.staticwebassets.runtime.json` using `Assembly.Location`. In single-file deployments and Native AOT (`PublishAot=true`), `Assembly.Location` returns an empty string for bundled/AOT assemblies and triggers three [IL3000](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/single-file/warnings/il3000) warnings:

```csharp
// src/Components/WebView/WebView/src/WebViewManager.cs
private sealed class StaticWebAssetsLoader
{
    internal static IFileProvider UseStaticWebAssets(IFileProvider fileProvider)
    {
        var manifestPath = ResolveRelativeToAssembly();
        if (File.Exists(manifestPath))
        {
            using var manifestStream = File.OpenRead(manifestPath);
            var manifest = ManifestStaticWebAssetFileProvider.StaticWebAssetManifest.Parse(manifestStream);
            if (manifest.ContentRoots.Length > 0)
            {
                var manifestProvider = new ManifestStaticWebAssetFileProvider(manifest, (path) => new PhysicalFileProvider(path));
                return new CompositeFileProvider(manifestProvider, fileProvider);
            }
        }

        return fileProvider;
    }

    private static string? ResolveRelativeToAssembly()
    {
        var assembly = Assembly.GetEntryAssembly();
        // warning IL3000: 'System.Reflection.Assembly.Location.get' always returns an empty string
        // for assemblies embedded in a single-file app. If the path to the app directory is needed,
        // consider calling 'System.AppContext.BaseDirectory'.
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(assembly?.Location)) // warning IL3000
        {
            return null;
        }

        var name = Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(assembly.Location); // warning IL3000

        return Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(assembly.Location)!, $"{name}.staticwebassets.runtime.json"); // warning IL3000
    }
}
```

Note that `<TargetName>.staticwebassets.runtime.json` is a development-time manifest. In the .NET SDK (`Microsoft.NET.Sdk.StaticWebAssets.targets`), `AddStaticWebAssetsManifest` copies it only to build output and explicitly excludes it from publish output:

```xml
<Target Name="AddStaticWebAssetsManifest" DependsOnTargets="ResolveStaticWebAssetsConfiguration">
  <ItemGroup>
    <ContentWithTargetPath Condition="Exists('$(StaticWebAssetDevelopmentManifestPath)')"
      Include="$(StaticWebAssetDevelopmentManifestPath)"
      TargetPath="$(TargetName).staticwebassets.runtime.json"
      CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest"
      CopyToPublishDirectory="Never" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Target>
```

Because `CopyToPublishDirectory="Never"`, published Native AOT and single-file apps normally do not contain this manifest at all (`File.Exists(manifestPath)` is `false`, and the original `fileProvider` is used). The goal is to eliminate the `IL3000` warnings cleanly without introducing unintended runtime behavior changes.

## In scope

- Eliminating `IL3000` warnings from `WebViewManager.StaticWebAssetsLoader.ResolveRelativeToAssembly()` under Native AOT (`PublishAot=true`) and clarifying expectations for single-file JIT (`PublishSingleFile=true`).
- Preserving existing static web assets resolution in development (JIT) builds and published Blazor Hybrid apps.

## Out of scope

- Broader Native AOT enablement for Blazor WebView (IPC serialization, `[JSInvokable]` source generation, component trimming annotations — tracked separately in #70863).
- Changing how `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.StaticWebAssets` packages published assets.

## Risks / unknowns

- **No public single-file feature switch:** `.NET` does not expose a `RuntimeFeature.IsSingleFile` switch. `RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported` is `false` for Native AOT, but remains `true` for single-file JIT (`PublishSingleFile=true`), and can also be `false` on non-Native-AOT runtimes (such as Mono full-AOT).
- **Runtime behavior changes with `AppContext.BaseDirectory`:** Switching to `AppContext.BaseDirectory` + `Assembly.GetName().Name` can resolve a different directory or file name than `Assembly.Location` and could cause a single-file or Native AOT app to load a manifest that it previously skipped (for example, if a manifest happens to sit next to the binary or in a custom/IDE `_IsPublishing=true` layout).
- **Analyzer vs. ILC behavior:** Guarding `Assembly.Location` with `RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported` lets ILC eliminate the branch under `PublishAot=true` (0 ILC warnings), but the Roslyn single-file analyzer (`EnableSingleFileAnalyzer=true` / `PublishSingleFile=true`) still reports `IL3000` on the retained branch when building WebView from source.
- **Unverified hosts:** We have not yet validated manifest behavior across all MAUI Blazor Hybrid targets (iOS, Mac Catalyst, Android, Windows) under both `dotnet build` and `dotnet publish`.

## Approaches explored

We tried several approaches while working on #70875, but did not settle on one yet because each has trade-offs:

### 1. Always resolve from `AppContext.BaseDirectory` and `Assembly.GetName().Name`

```csharp
private static string? ResolveRelativeToAssembly()
{
    var assembly = Assembly.GetEntryAssembly();
    var name = assembly?.GetName().Name;
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(name))
    {
        return null;
    }

    return Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, $"{name}.staticwebassets.runtime.json");
}
```

- **Pros:** Removes `Assembly.Location` completely; produces 0 `IL3000` warnings in both Native AOT (`PublishAot=true`) and single-file JIT (`PublishSingleFile=true`) with no suppressions.
- **Cons:** Changes runtime lookup semantics for all apps (`AppContext.BaseDirectory` vs. `Path.GetDirectoryName(assembly.Location)`, and `GetName().Name` vs. filename without extension). Also changes single-file and Native AOT apps from skipping the lookup to probing `AppContext.BaseDirectory`.

### 2. Feature-guard with `RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported` and fall back to `AppContext.BaseDirectory`

```csharp
private static string? ResolveRelativeToAssembly()
{
    var assembly = Assembly.GetEntryAssembly();
    if (assembly is null)
    {
        return null;
    }

    var (directory, name) = GetDirectoryAndName(assembly);
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(directory) || string.IsNullOrEmpty(name))
    {
        return null;
    }

    return Path.Combine(directory, $"{name}.staticwebassets.runtime.json");
}

private static (string? Directory, string? Name) GetDirectoryAndName(Assembly assembly)
{
    if (RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(assembly.Location)) // warning IL3000 under PublishSingleFile (trimmed by ILC under PublishAot)
        {
            return (null, null);
        }

        return (
            Path.GetDirectoryName(assembly.Location), // warning IL3000 under PublishSingleFile (trimmed by ILC under PublishAot)
            Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(assembly.Location)); // warning IL3000 under PublishSingleFile (trimmed by ILC under PublishAot)
    }

    return (AppContext.BaseDirectory, assembly.GetName().Name);
}
```

- **Pros:** Keeps JIT and single-file JIT behavior identical to `main`. Under `PublishAot=true`, ILC substitutes `IsDynamicCodeSupported` with `false` and trims the `Assembly.Location` branch, yielding **0 ILC warnings** without needing `[UnconditionalSuppressMessage]`.
- **Cons:** In a local Native AOT static-web-assets publish test, `AppContext.BaseDirectory` pointed to `publish/`, where `*.staticwebassets.runtime.json` does not exist (`CopyToPublishDirectory="Never"`), so the fallback never found a manifest in normal publish output while still introducing a subtle behavior difference if one is present. Single-file JIT builds (`PublishSingleFile=true`) also still get 3 `IL3000` warnings from the Roslyn single-file analyzer.

### 3. Return `null` when `!RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported`

```csharp
private static string? ResolveRelativeToAssembly()
{
    if (!RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported)
    {
        return null;
    }

    var assembly = Assembly.GetEntryAssembly();
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(assembly?.Location)) // warning IL3000 under PublishSingleFile (trimmed by ILC under PublishAot)
    {
        return null;
    }

    var name = Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(assembly.Location); // warning IL3000 under PublishSingleFile (trimmed by ILC under PublishAot)

    return Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(assembly.Location)!, $"{name}.staticwebassets.runtime.json"); // warning IL3000 under PublishSingleFile (trimmed by ILC under PublishAot)
}
```

- **Pros:** Minimal diff, no `[UnconditionalSuppressMessage]`, 0 ILC warnings under `PublishAot=true`, and preserves the existing behavior of skipping the development manifest in Native AOT publish output.
- **Cons:** Still emits 3 `IL3000` warnings under `PublishSingleFile=true` when the single-file analyzer runs on WebView source (since `IsDynamicCodeSupported` is `true` for single-file JIT). Also skips manifest lookup on other runtimes where `IsDynamicCodeSupported` is `false`.

### 4. Explicitly suppress `IL3000` (or gate behind a dedicated feature switch / host opt-in)

```csharp
[UnconditionalSuppressMessage("SingleFile", "IL3000:Assembly.Location",
    Justification = "The static web assets runtime manifest is a development-only file not copied to publish output. Returning null when Assembly.Location is empty is the intended behavior for single-file and Native AOT apps.")]
private static string? ResolveRelativeToAssembly()
{
    var assembly = Assembly.GetEntryAssembly();
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(assembly?.Location))
    {
        return null;
    }

    var name = Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(assembly.Location);

    return Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(assembly.Location)!, $"{name}.staticwebassets.runtime.json");
}
```

- **Pros:** Preserves exact runtime behavior everywhere and silences `IL3000` in both ILC (`PublishAot=true`) and the Roslyn single-file analyzer (`PublishSingleFile=true`). Alternatively, a dedicated MSBuild/runtime feature switch (or moving development-manifest registration to the host/dev-only path) could strip the loader entirely in published apps without relying on `IsDynamicCodeSupported`.
- **Cons:** Relying on `[UnconditionalSuppressMessage]` requires agreement that suppressing `IL3000` on `Assembly.Location` is acceptable here; a dedicated feature switch or host-level opt-in adds new configuration surface.

## Examples / local reproduction

The `IL3000` warnings can be reproduced locally (tested on macOS arm64 with SDK `12.0.100-alpha.1.26571.102`):

1. **Single-file analyzer on the WebView project directly:**

```bash
source activate.sh
dotnet build src/Components/WebView/WebView/src/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebView.csproj \
  -p:BuildNodeJS=false \
  -p:IncludeComponentsWebAssets=false \
  -p:EnableSingleFileAnalyzer=true \
  -p:IsAotCompatible=true
```

This fails with 3 `IL3000` diagnostics in `WebViewManager.cs`.

2. **Single-file JIT publish (`PublishSingleFile=true`) referencing the WebView project:**

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net12.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <FrameworkReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.App" />
    <ProjectReference Include="/path/to/aspnetcore/src/Components/WebView/WebView/src/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebView.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

```csharp
using System.Reflection;
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebView;

var loader = typeof(WebViewManager).GetNestedType("StaticWebAssetsLoader", BindingFlags.NonPublic)!;
var resolve = loader.GetMethod("ResolveRelativeToAssembly", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Static)!;
Console.WriteLine($"Dynamic code supported: {RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported}");
Console.WriteLine($"Manifest path: {resolve.Invoke(null, null) ?? "<null>"}");
```

```bash
source activate.sh
dotnet publish /path/to/Probe.csproj -c Debug -r osx-arm64 --self-contained true \
  -p:PublishSingleFile=true -p:BuildNodeJS=false -p:IncludeComponentsWebAssets=false \
  -p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=false --nologo -v:quiet
```

This emits the 3 `IL3000` warnings from `WebViewManager.cs` (even with Approach 3 applied) and prints `Dynamic code supported: True` / `Manifest path: <null>` at runtime. Publishing the same method with `PublishAot=true` produces 3 `IL3000` warnings from ILC without a guard, and 0 ILC warnings with the `RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported` guard.

Issues.Title: [release/11.0] Fix Blazor browser option handling
Issues.Body:
Backport of #70526 to release/11.0

/cc @ilonatommy @dariatiurina

# Fix Blazor browser option handling

Fix five server-configured browser option issues.

## Description

Backports #70526, which fixes the five `WithBrowserOptions` problems reported in #70510. The circuit inactivity timeout is read when circuit disposal is scheduled instead of being captured during boot. The server-configured WebAssembly culture is forwarded before the runtime loads, and an explicit JavaScript culture still takes precedence. `PreserveDom = false` now disables enhanced navigation for links and forms and replaces streamed and enhanced POST content, and a GET that first supplies the setting falls back to a full page load. The server log level is applied unless startup or an initializer sets the circuit log level explicitly. Reconnection retry intervals shorter than one second now take effect.

The production changes apply without conflicts. Conflicts in `BrowserConfigurationTest.cs` and `RazorComponentEndpointsStartup.cs` were resolved by omitting the `EnvironmentName` test setup and assertions from #69702, which is not in release/11.0.

Fixes #70510

## Customer Impact

Applications that configure these options through `WithBrowserOptions` in .NET 11 do not get the documented behavior, and no error is reported. The circuit inactivity timeout, WebAssembly culture, DOM preservation setting, and circuit log level are ignored, and short reconnection intervals are not honored. The behavior is documented in dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs#38107. The workaround is to set the equivalent values in JavaScript startup options.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

`WithBrowserOptions` is new in .NET 11.

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [x] Medium
- [ ] Low

The change spans the Blazor boot, enhanced navigation, streaming, and reconnection code paths. Applications on 11.0 that already set `PreserveDom = false` currently keep enhanced navigation and will instead get full page loads and DOM replacement after this change, which matches the documented behavior but is an observable change. The other four fixes only take effect when the corresponding option is configured, and explicit JavaScript or initializer values keep precedence over server configuration.

## Verification

- [ ] Manual (required)
- [x] Automated

#70526 adds E2E and unit coverage for each option, and this backport carries those tests.

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

No packaging configuration files are changed.

Issues.Title: Fix Blazor event dispatch diagnostics for null-delegate callbacks
Issues.Body:
# Fix Blazor event dispatch diagnostics for null-delegate callbacks

Prevents NullReferenceException during Blazor event dispatch diagnostics. Occurs when an event callback has a receiver but its delegate is null. Also covers the linked report involving a nullable Action bound to onmouseleave.

### Root Cause

A valid EventCallback can retain its receiver while containing a null delegate. Tracing and metrics accessed callback.Delegate.Target and .Method without checking the delegate. Event invocation supports null delegates, but diagnostic metadata collection could throw.

### Solution

Use null-conditional access for callback.Delegate?.Target and callback.Delegate?.Method. Apply the guards to tracing, event-duration metrics, and synchronous failure metrics. Preserve existing event dispatch behavior without requiring application-level no-op handlers.

### Test Case Coverage

All 4 focused null-delegate tests and 150 renderer tests passed. A temporary managed-renderer probe covered nullable hover callbacks across four combinations. The scoped Components build succeeded; browser E2E and pre-fix red verification were not run.

Fixes #69459

Issues.Title: [Review agent] Follow stale owner references when teardown fails before replacement (#70495)
Issues.Body:
## Summary

On [dotnet/aspnetcore#70495](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70495), head `56d857dbd2bb7ea93a7698938c7f075b70edeea7`, [hosted `/review` with `code-review`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70495#discussion_r4700846890) found that a failed page reload can leave a disposed service scope reachable from host dispatch.

## Source evidence

At [`PageContext.cs:70`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/56d857dbd2bb7ea93a7698938c7f075b70edeea7/src/Components/WebView/WebView/src/PageContext.cs#L55-L80), the renderer-failure path now disposes the scope and rethrows. The reload exits before `AttachToPageAsync` replaces `_currentPageContext`; the manager itself is not disposed. `TryDispatchAsync` can still dispatch a callback against the old page, and resolving a scoped service can throw. The old failure path did not dispose that scope.

Neither local skill reported this path: both local `code-review` and local `review-pull-request` instead flagged repeat manager disposal after dispatcher shutdown, a different trigger and consequence. The [same-head native CCR review](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70495#pullrequestreview-6064013574) did not report the stale context and predates the skill landing. The earlier local comparison reviewed a different head.

## Proposed fix

For changes that add cleanup on a throwing path, follow each caller past the failed await: identify which owner references still point to the resource, and which subsequent operations can pass the owner's guards and use it. Treat exceptional reload and final manager disposal as separate cases.

Tracked under dotnet/aspnetcore#70231.

## Summary

On [dotnet/aspnetcore#70741](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70741), head `37529818a9e204cd8b6303b10a5fb85d1904573a`, hosted `/review` with `code-review` published a [medium finding](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70741#discussion_r4701134351) about redundant provider requests. The calibration gap is demonstrated; the product claim is not disproved.

## Source evidence

At [`Virtualize.cs:993`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/37529818a9e204cd8b6303b10a5fb85d1904573a/src/Components/Web/src/Virtualization/Virtualize.cs#L993), an uncountable retained iterator can take the rendered-count fallback. An enlarged same-start measurement could then re-fetch rows the iterator already covers **if** it arrives while the one-shot skip is still armed. The managed branch does not establish that the real browser produces and delivers that measurement in the required order. The lazy-result and countable-overdelivery tests do not establish that combination.

Local `review-pull-request` surfaced the same candidate and kept it unresolved; local `code-review` did not report it. [Native CCR](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70741#discussion_r4701015051) raised a different request-settling coverage concern, not the lazy re-fetch on this head. The earlier local comparison reviewed a different head.

## Proposed fix

Keep runtime claims unresolved when a managed callback demonstrates a branch but bypasses the producer of a required browser event or ordering. Promote only when the event order is established by an applicable contract or by observing the real producer and provider request count.

## Summary

On [dotnet/aspnetcore#70810](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70810), head `49aec2060a1bb80df854d8565710115c383e4b1e`, neither [hosted `/review` with `code-review`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/45713556679) nor [native CCR](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70810#pullrequestreview-6065771082) reported that the changed assertion can lose browser failure diagnostics.

## Source evidence

At [`VirtualizationTest.cs:6953–6976`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/49aec2060a1bb80df854d8565710115c383e4b1e/src/Components/test/E2ETest/Tests/VirtualizationTest.cs#L6953-L6976), `Browser.True` can return when the offset stabilizes, then the separate xUnit assertion fails at line 6975 if the settled offset is out of tolerance. That failure bypasses `WaitAssert`'s timeout reporting (including screenshot, DOM, and console diagnostics) for a mismatch that stays out of tolerance. This is separate from the existing advisory about an offset that later recovers.

Local `code-review` verified the diagnostic loss. Local `review-pull-request` found the same path but marked it unresolved pending browser geometry and polling evidence. That evidence could establish how often the branch is reached, but is not needed to show which reporting path the assertion uses when it fails. The earlier local comparison reviewed a different head.

## Proposed fix

Compare failure diagnostics as well as pass/fail behavior when assertions cross helper boundaries. Separate the source-proven consequence on a failed assertion from the frequency or reproducibility of the browser state that triggers it.

Issues.Title: [Review agent] Check whether a replacement stylesheet can take over before retaining the outgoing stylesheet (#70743)
Issues.Body:
## Summary

On [dotnet/aspnetcore#70743](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70743), head `24b8fae3d30971e53ce2e2502cc48908ac0a03b4`, native Copilot Code Review (CCR) [recommended approval](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70743#pullrequestreview-6065616036) without reporting two ways a same-ID replacement can leave stale screen styles active.

## Source evidence

At [`HeadStylesheetTransition.ts:54–70`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/24b8fae3d30971e53ce2e2502cc48908ac0a03b4/src/Components/Web.JS/src/Rendering/HeadStylesheetTransition.ts#L54-L70), the guard admits an enabled same-ID replacement with no sheet. It does not check whether the incoming stylesheet applies to the current media or even has an `href`. A pending print-only stylesheet cannot replace screen styles; an `href`-less link does not start a stylesheet load. The old screen link remains active while cleanup waits for completion or the fallback timer. The previous behavior removed the outgoing link.

Hosted `/review` with `code-review` [caught the print-only case](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70743#discussion_r4701516905) and did not report the missing-`href` case. Local `code-review` did the reverse. Local `review-pull-request` did not report the print-only case and retained missing `href` as unresolved, not verified. The earlier local comparison reviewed a different head.

## Proposed fix

When reviewing a handoff, check that the replacement can produce the awaited event and take over the outgoing resource's effect. Cover both triggers as variants of one eligibility defect; use the relevant HTML loading contract where it establishes what the browser will do.

Tracked under dotnet/aspnetcore#70231.

Issues.Title: EphemeralDataProtectionProvider: Unprotect fails for an empty payload on .NET 11 (Windows)
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

On .NET 11.0.0 on Windows, a protector created from `EphemeralDataProtectionProvider` cannot unprotect the output of `Protect` for an empty byte array. `Unprotect` throws `CryptographicException: The payload was invalid` from `CngGcmAuthenticatedEncryptor.Decrypt`. Payloads of 1 and 16 bytes round-trip. The same code works on .NET 10 and on Linux with .NET 11.

It fails on every run (20 of 20, new provider and purpose each time). A provider using a persisted key ring (`AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToFileSystem(...)`) round-trips the empty payload on .NET 11, with both AES_256_CBC and AES_256_GCM.

### Expected Behavior

`protector.Unprotect(protector.Protect(Array.Empty<byte>()))` returns an empty array, as on .NET 10.

### Steps To Reproduce

Save as `probe.cs` and run `dotnet run --file probe.cs` (use `net10.0` for the .NET 10 comparison):

```csharp
#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
#:property TargetFramework=net11.0
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection;

Console.WriteLine($"Runtime {Environment.Version}; DP asm {typeof(IDataProtector).Assembly.GetName().Version}");
var p = new EphemeralDataProtectionProvider().CreateProtector("p");
foreach (var len in new[] { 0, 1, 16 })
{
    var ct = p.Protect(new byte[len]);
    Console.Write($"len {len}: ciphertext {ct.Length} bytes; ");
    try { Console.WriteLine($"unprotect OK {p.Unprotect(ct).Length}"); }
    catch (Exception ex) { Console.WriteLine($"unprotect THREW {ex.GetType().FullName}: {ex.Message}\n{ex.StackTrace}"); }
}
```

Windows 11 x64 (10.0.26300), SDK 11.0.100, runtime 11.0.0:

```text
Runtime 11.0.0; DP asm 11.0.0.0
len 0: ciphertext 64 bytes; unprotect THREW System.Security.Cryptography.CryptographicException: The payload was invalid. For more information go to https://aka.ms/aspnet/dataprotectionwarning
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.Cng.CngGcmAuthenticatedEncryptor.Decrypt(ArraySegment`1 ciphertext, ArraySegment`1 additionalAuthenticatedData)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.KeyRingBasedDataProtector.UnprotectCore(Byte[] protectedData, Boolean allowOperationsOnRevokedKeys, UnprotectStatus& status)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.KeyRingBasedDataProtector.Unprotect(Byte[] protectedData)
   at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in probe.cs:line 11
len 1: ciphertext 65 bytes; unprotect OK 1
len 16: ciphertext 80 bytes; unprotect OK 16
```

Windows 11 x64, SDK 10.0.404, runtime 10.0.15 (`net10.0`):

```text
Runtime 10.0.15; DP asm 10.0.0.0
len 0: ciphertext 64 bytes; unprotect OK 0
len 1: ciphertext 65 bytes; unprotect OK 1
len 16: ciphertext 80 bytes; unprotect OK 16
```

Linux x64 (`mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:11.0`, Ubuntu 26.04, SDK 11.0.100, runtime 11.0.0), 5 runs, all identical:

```text
Runtime 11.0.0; DP asm 11.0.0.0
len 0: ciphertext 100 bytes; unprotect OK 0
len 1: ciphertext 100 bytes; unprotect OK 1
len 16: ciphertext 116 bytes; unprotect OK 16
```

Linux x64 (`mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0`, Ubuntu 24.04, SDK 10.0.201, runtime 10.0.5, `net10.0`): all three lengths OK.

`Protect` of an empty array produces 64 bytes on Windows on both .NET 10 and .NET 11; only `Unprotect` differs. On Windows the ephemeral protector uses AES-256-GCM through CNG (`CngGcmAuthenticatedEncryptor`); on Linux it produces CBC-sized payloads (100 bytes for lengths 0 and 1).

### Exceptions (if any)

`System.Security.Cryptography.CryptographicException: The payload was invalid.` Stack trace above.

### .NET Version

11.0.100 (runtime 11.0.0). Works on 10.0.404 (runtime 10.0.15).

### Anything else?

Only observed with `EphemeralDataProtectionProvider` on Windows, and only for the empty payload. macOS not tested.

Production initialization and API design, robust component metadata/preservation, permanent publish-time/NativeAOT coverage, and cross-runtime/platform validation remain required. The extracted generator layer also needs production packaging, remaining framework registrations and generic/metadata scenarios; existing prototype diagnostics JSI0001–JSI0006 do not establish completeness. Committed browser/renderer-event coverage, iOS/Android/Windows, the complete render-mode matrix, and a full-repository build have not been validated. Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json
Issues.Body:
I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json" (#1067)

The is a problem nesting embedded resources.  I was experimenting with nesting .cshtml files using the existing rules and did this:

Modal.cs (bootstrap modal web component)
   -> Modal.cs.cshtml (it's view file)

`Modal.cs.cshtml` is set to Embedded Resource, and clearly shows it, but is completed IGNORED by the build process (simply open the DLL in a text editor [such as Notepad++] and scroll to the bottom and look for text).  If I rename the file to "Modal.cshtml" instead it works perfectly fine!  :/  I don't think whether or not a file is embedded should have and role in excluding a file from being embedded so this seems like a bug to me.

Yes, I'm aware of upcoming nesting controls in v15.6, but I'm not able to install it yet, and regardless, this should work fine, so it should be looked into nonetheless.

Just to add: I'm using wild-cards to include the file.  If I explicitly add it I get this:

`Duplicate 'EmbeddedResource' items were included. ...`

So it's clearly found.  It's obviously something up with the build process not finding the nested file.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

## Current support policy

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Title: Add automation to create docs tracking issues for breaking changes
Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

## Security

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

### Discussion

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and MVC API analyzers are deprecated
Issues.Body:
## Description

The `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` MSBuild property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. When `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will now emit warning `ASPDEPR007`.

## Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

## Previous behavior

Previously, developers could set `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` in their Web SDK projects to enable MVC API analyzers without any warnings or deprecation notices.

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

The project would build successfully without any deprecation warnings.

## New behavior

Starting in .NET 10 Preview 7, when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will emit warning `ASPDEPR007`:

```
warning ASPDEPR007: The IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
```

The analyzers will continue to function, but developers will receive this deprecation warning during compilation.

## Type of breaking change

- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

## Reason for change

## Reason for change

The MVC API analyzers were originally introduced to help keep return types and attributes in sync for API controllers, ensuring consistency between method signatures and their corresponding OpenAPI documentation. These analyzers provided compile-time validation to catch mismatches between declared return types and the actual types returned by controller actions.

However, with the introduction of Minimal APIs and the `TypedResults` pattern, the .NET ecosystem has evolved toward a more type-safe approach for API development. `TypedResults` provides compile-time guarantees about response types without requiring additional analyzers, making the MVC API analyzers redundant for modern .NET applications. In .NET 10, `TypedResults` are supported in controller-based APIs.

**Previous approach with MVC API analyzers:**
```csharp
[HttpGet]
[ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)]
[ProducesResponseType(404)]
public async Task<ActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    if (product == null)
        return NotFound(); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType(404)
    
    return Ok(product); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)
}
```

**Or with controller actions using TypedResults:**
```csharp
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    return product == null 
        ? TypedResults.NotFound() 
        : TypedResults.Ok(product);
}
```

The `TypedResults` pattern eliminates the need for separate analyzers because the return type itself (`Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>`) explicitly declares all possible response types at compile time. This approach is more maintainable, provides better IntelliSense support, and automatically generates accurate OpenAPI documentation without additional tooling.

As the .NET ecosystem continues to embrace `TypedResults` as the recommended pattern for API development, the MVC API analyzers have become obsolete and are being deprecated to streamline the development experience.

## Recommended action

Developers should:

1. **Remove the deprecated property**: Remove `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` from your project files to eliminate the warning.

2. **Suppress the warning temporarily**: If you need to continue using the deprecated analyzers temporarily, you can suppress the warning:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ASPDEPR007</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

3. **Migrate to TypedResults**: Migrate to the `TypedResults` pattern documented above to ensure better consistency between application behavior and OpenAPI documentation.

## Affected APIs

- MSBuild property: `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers`
- Associated MVC API analyzers included when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is `true`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Forwarded Headers Middleware Now Ignores X-Forwarded-* Headers from Unknown Proxies
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 8.0.17 and 9.0.6, the Forwarded Headers Middleware will ignore all `X-Forwarded-*` headers from proxies that are not explicitly configured as trusted.

### Version

.NET 8

### Previous behavior

Previously, the middleware, when not configured to use `X-Forwarded-For`, would process `X-Forwarded-Prefix`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and `X-Forwarded-Host` headers from any source, potentially allowing malicious or misconfigured proxies/clients to spoof these headers and affect your application's understanding of client information.

### New behavior

With this change, only headers sent by known, trusted proxies (as configured via `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies` and `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownNetworks`) will be processed. Headers from unknown sources will be ignored.

**This is a breaking change**: If your deployment relied on forwarded headers from proxies not configured in your application's trusted proxy list, those headers will no longer be honored.

This can cause behavior like infinite redirects if you're using the Https redirection middleware and using TLS termination in your proxy. Or authentication to fail if using TLS termination and expecting an https request.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The change was made for security hardening, as the proxy and IP lists weren't being applied in all cases.

### Recommended action

- **Review your deployment topology:**  
  Ensure that all legitimate proxy servers in front of your app are properly added to `KnownProxies` or `KnownNetworks` in your `ForwardedHeadersOptions` configuration.
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownProxies = { IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_PROXY_IP") }
  });
  ```
  Or, for a network:
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownNetworks = { new IPNetwork(IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_NETWORK_IP"), PREFIX_LENGTH) }
  });
  ```

- **If you wish to enable previous behavior:**  
  You may need to relax your configuration, but this is **not recommended** due to security risks. You can do this by clearing the `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies` lists in `ForwardedHeadersOptions` to allow any proxy or network to forward these headers.

You can also set the `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` environment variable to true, which clears the lists and enables `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto`.

For applications targeting .NET 9.0 or less, you can set the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpOverrides.IgnoreUnknownProxiesWithoutFor` [AppContext](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/runtime-libraries/system-appcontext) switch to `"true"` or `1` to get back to the previous behavior. Alternatively, set the `MICROSOFT_ASPNETCORE_HTTPOVERRIDES_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_PROXIES_WITHOUT_FOR` environment variable.

> [!Note]
> In cloud environments, the proxy IP(s) can change over the lifetime of the app and `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` is sometimes used to make forwarded headers work.

### References

- [Forwarded Headers Middleware documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/host-and-deploy/proxy-load-balancer)

### Affected APIs

`UseForwardedHeaders();`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: dev cert export no longer creates folder
Issues.Body:
### Description

When you export the ASP.NET Core development certificate (used to enable https in local development), it will no longer create the directory into which the certificate is being exported, if that directory doesn’t already exist.

This change first appears in 8.0.10 and 9.0 RC1.

### Version

.NET 8 GA

### Previous behavior

```
dotnet dev-certs https -ep C:\NonExistent\cert.pfx
```

If `C:\NonExistent\` did not exist when the command was run, it would be created (with permissions inherited from the containing directory).

### New behavior

The target directory must exist or the export will fail with a message like `There was an error exporting the HTTPS developer certificate to a file.`

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The development certificate is exported with its private key, so unauthorized access can be very problematic.  It may, nevertheless, be necessary to make it readable to multiple accounts - e.g. if the consuming process will not be run as the current user.  Rather than attempting to determine (and securely establish) permissions for the target directory, `dotnet dev-certs` require that it already exist.

### Recommended action

Create the target directory (with appropriate permissions) before invoking `dotnet dev-certs`.

### Affected APIs

This functionality is not presently exposed via an API - it is invoked from the command line.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Handling of middleware types with multiple constructors
Issues.Body:
### Description

Formerly, when a middleware type with multiple satisfiable constructors was instantiated from the dependency injection container, the one with the most parameters would be used.  Now that only happens if the dependency injection container implements [`IServiceProviderIsService`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.iserviceproviderisservice).

### Version

.NET 9 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Formerly, the first constructor was preferred (when both were satisfied) because it has more parameters.

```csharp
public class CookiePolicyMiddleware
{
    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options, ILoggerFactory factory)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }

    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }
}
```

### New behavior

Now, neither constructor is preferred and construction fails with an error like 
```
System.InvalidOperationException: 'Multiple constructors accepting all given argument types have been found in type 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware'. There should only be one applicable constructor.'
```

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The activation mechanism was [changed](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/55722) to help support keyed dependency injection.

### Recommended action

If this happens and you can't upgrade to a dependency injection container that implements `IServiceProviderIsService`, you can add `ActivatorUtilitiesConstructorAttribute` to the preferred constructor of the affected middleware type.

### Affected APIs

This is [known](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/57231) to cause errors when instantiating `Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware` with [Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection) 7.x.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey has a slightly altered meaning
Issues.Body:
### Description

`DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey` no longer reflects whether the default key is close to its expiration time.

### Version

.NET 9 Preview 3

### Previous behavior

It was an undocumented, but consistent, feature of the API that `ShouldGenerateNewKey` would be true if the default key was within two days (an over-simplification) of its expiration time.  The amount of lead time was based on the polling interval of `ICacheableKeyRingProvider`, which was not something `IDefaultKeyResolver.ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy` should have depended upon (since, for example, alternative implementations would probably not be aware of these details).

### New behavior

If `ShouldGenerateNewKey` is true, it now indicates that either there is no default key or that for some other policy reason (i.e. in a specialized implementation of `IDefaultKeyResolver`, a new key should be generated.  The `ICacheableKeyRingProvider` will make its own decision about whether the expiration time is close enough to warrant generating a new key.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

First, we wanted to change the logic around key generation near expiration time and, second, this makes it more straightforward to implement a custom `IDefaultKeyResolver`.

Note that the documentation for this type already states that "This API supports infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases."

### Recommended action

If you have an `IDefaultKeyResolver` implementation that tries to replicate the expiry logic, that logic can be removed (however, leaving it is fine as well).

If you were consuming `IDefaultKeyResolver` directly, for the express purpose of determining whether expiration was pending and that continues to be important, you can the default key's `ExpirationDate` property directly.

### Affected APIs

Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal.DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Minimal APIs consuming IFormFile or IFormFileCollection parameters require anti-forgery checks
Issues.Body:
### Description

Minimal API endpoints that consume an `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` will now be opted-in to requiring anti-forgery token validation using the new anti-forgery middleware.

### Version

.NET 8 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did not require anti-forgery validation.

### New behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did require anti-forgery validation. An exception will be thrown if the anti-forgery middleware is not registered for an API that defines these input types.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Anti-forgery token validation is a recommended security precaution for APIs that consume data from a form.

### Recommended action

Users can opt out of anti-forgery validation for specific endpoints by using the `DisableAntiforgery` method like so:

```csharp
var app = WebApplication.Create();

app.MapPost("/", (IFormFile formFile) => ...)
  .DisableAntiforgery();

app.Run();
```

### Affected APIs

None.
